client: I've been really struggling since my grandmother passed away last month. Every time I try to sit down and get work done, these memories of her just come flooding in and I can't concentrate on anything. I'm not even sure talking about it is going to help, because it's not like anything can actually change what happened.
therapist: It sounds like you're carrying a deep sadness right now, and it makes complete sense that grief would spill into every corner of your life, including your ability to focus. You're right that nothing can change what happened, and I want to gently offer that talking isn't about changing the past — it can be about helping you find a way to carry it that feels a little less heavy. I'm curious, when those memories of her come flooding in, what kinds of thoughts tend to follow them?

client: When the memories come, I usually end up thinking that I should have visited more, that I kept putting it off because life got busy, and now there's just... nothing I can do about it. It's like my brain won't let me just miss her — it always has to turn it into this indictment of what a terrible granddaughter I was. I know on some level that's not totally fair, but it feels completely true in those moments.
therapist: That self-critical voice — turning grief into a verdict about who you are as a person — is so common in loss, and yet it can feel so convincing in the moment, even when a quieter part of you senses it isn't the whole truth. What you just said is really important: you *know* it doesn't feel totally fair, which means there's another perspective in there trying to be heard. I'd love to explore that with you — what do you think your grandmother would have said about the kind of granddaughter you were?

client: I've been sitting with that question for a second, and honestly it makes me want to cry a little, because I think she would have said I was a good granddaughter. But then my brain immediately jumps to "well, she had to say that, she loved you" — like I can't even let myself have that without tearing it down. It's exhausting, always finding a way to make the kind thing feel less true than the harsh thing.
therapist: What you just described — that exhausting pattern of dismantling every gentle thought before it can land — is actually a really important thing to notice about yourself, and it takes courage to see it so clearly. It's worth asking: if a close friend dismissed every kind thing said about them by saying "they had to say that," you'd probably recognize that as unfair to them — so what makes your grandmother's genuine love for you less valid as evidence than your harshest self-judgments? What do you think it would feel like to let her view of you carry just as much weight as the critical voice?

client: I hear what you're saying, and honestly, the friend analogy kind of stopped me for a second because you're right, I would never let a friend do that to themselves. But when I try to apply it to me, there's this immediate wall that goes up, like my brain just says "that's different, you're different." I guess it would feel... quieter, maybe, if I let her see me the way she does, but I'm also scared that if I lean into that, I'm just setting myself up to feel the loss of her more when she's gone.
therapist: That fear makes so much sense — like allowing yourself to feel fully loved by her means opening a door to how much her absence hurts, and right now that feels like a risk your heart isn't sure it can take. But I want to gently reflect something back: she *is* already gone, and you're already feeling that loss deeply — so that quieter, softer version of yourself that she saw isn't something you'd be losing, it's actually something she left *with* you. I wonder — what might it mean to carry her loving view of you not as a reminder of what's gone, but as something she gave you that's still here?

client: That's... a really different way of looking at it, and part of me wants to hold onto it, but another part just feels like I'd be fooling myself. Like, if I start thinking of her gentle view of me as something she "gave" me, what if I lose that too, the way I lose everything eventually? It almost feels safer to just keep it locked away where nothing can touch it or take it from me.
therapist: There's something really tender in what you just shared — this instinct to protect the most precious things by keeping them locked away, because love and loss have started to feel like the same thing. But I want to sit with this gently: keeping her view of you locked away to protect it might also mean never actually getting to *feel* it, which is its own kind of loss. What would it look like to let yourself hold it, even just a little, not as something that can be taken, but as something already woven into who you are?

client: I hear what you're saying, and part of me wants to believe that's possible, but it feels really risky. Like if I start letting myself actually feel how much my mom believed in me, I'm also letting in how much I miss her, and I don't know if I can hold both of those things at once without falling apart. It's easier to keep it at a distance than to risk that.
therapist: It sounds like you're in a quieter, more reflective place right now — not in crisis, but sitting with something that feels genuinely fragile and uncertain. I want to offer something gently: "falling apart" sounds terrifying, but what if it's not the opposite of holding yourself together — what if allowing yourself to feel both her love and your grief, even in small doses, is actually how you *do* hold yourself together, rather than how you lose it? I'm wondering, has there ever been a moment in your life where you let yourself feel something really hard and discovered you were more capable of surviving it than you expected?

client: I hear what you're saying, and part of me wants to believe it... but it also feels a little too neat, like a reframe that sounds good in theory but might not hold up when I'm actually alone at 2am missing her. I think there was one time, after my dad got sick, where I cried for what felt like hours and somehow woke up the next morning still functioning, still me. But with my grandmother it feels different, heavier somehow, like the grief is tangled up with guilt because I didn't visit as much as I should have in her last year.
therapist: That skepticism is actually really healthy — a reframe that only works in the therapy room isn't much use to you at 2am, and I don't want to offer you something that feels hollow when it matters most. What you said about your dad is so significant though: you *did* survive hours of that kind of pain and woke up still yourself, which means some part of you already knows how to move through grief — and I wonder if what makes this feel heavier is less about the grief itself and more about that guilt making it feel like you don't *deserve* to heal from it. What do you think — is the guilt acting like a kind of punishment you feel you owe her?

client: That question kind of stopped me cold, honestly. Because yeah, I think maybe it is — like if I let myself feel better, it means I'm saying what happened between us didn't matter, or that I'm just moving on and leaving her behind. And some part of me feels like staying in the pain is the only way I can still show her that she mattered to me.
therapist: What you just named is so important, and it takes real clarity to see it that way — that the pain has become a way of staying loyal to her, of saying *she mattered*. But I want to offer this gently: is it possible that healing isn't leaving her behind, but actually learning to carry her with you in a way that lets you live fully — which might be exactly what someone who loved you would want for you? What do you think she would say if she knew you were holding onto the pain as a way of honoring her?

client: I've thought about that before, actually, and I know she'd probably tell me to stop being so stubborn and go live my life. But knowing what she'd say and actually being able to do it feel like completely different things — like there's this gap between my head and my heart that I can't seem to close. And honestly, part of me worries that if I stop hurting, I'll just... forget her, or she'll feel further away somehow.
therapist: That gap between knowing something and truly *feeling* it is one of the most human experiences there is, and it doesn't mean you're failing — it means grief takes time to move through, not just understand. What strikes me is that you already carry her so vividly — her voice, what she'd say, how she'd roll her eyes at your stubbornness — and that *is* her, still present in you, which is almost the opposite of forgetting. I'm curious, when you imagine a version of yourself six months from now who is living more fully, do you picture her as someone who has forgotten her grandmother, or someone who has found a way to bring her along?

client: That question kind of stopped me for a second, because honestly my first instinct was to feel defensive, like you were trying to trick me into being okay with losing her. But when I actually sat with it... I guess the version of me I'd want to be isn't someone who's moved on, it's someone who carries her without it feeling like carrying a wound all the time. I just don't know how you get from here to there, and part of me worries that if the pain starts to ease, it means I loved her less.
therapist: That image you just created — carrying her without it feeling like carrying a wound — is genuinely beautiful, and it came from *you*, which tells me your heart already knows something your fear hasn't quite caught up to yet. And I want to gently challenge that last worry: the intensity of pain isn't what measures love — you could meet someone tomorrow who is decades out from losing someone dear and loves them just as fiercely, just more peacefully. What if the love actually stays constant, and what changes over time is just how much space the grief takes up alongside it?
